title: Rush Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Rush wells have a 280-foot median depth; see typical yield, water levels, drilling costs, and local permit history.
h1: Rush, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost Guide
intro_html:
Buying land or planning a home near Rush means understanding what nearby wells actually produce. In the Colorado Division of Water Resources records reviewed here, permitted wells within five miles of Rush commonly reach several hundred feet, with most reported yields falling between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

The records include domestic, household, and stock wells, along with wells in fractured bedrock, Laramie Fox Hills, and Pierre Shale settings. These figures are useful for budgeting and comparison, but they do not guarantee what a new well will encounter on a particular lot. Check nearby well construction reports, water rights, septic locations, and current permit requirements before closing or starting site work.

sections.heading: Rush well depths and the ground below
sections.html:
Rush wells have a median reported depth of 280 feet. The middle half runs from 175 to 360 feet, while the 90th percentile reaches 475 feet. That spread matters when you request a drilling bid: a lot with a 280-foot estimate should not be priced the same as one where nearby wells approach 475 feet.

Depth records are concentrated in the 100-to-300-foot and 300-to-600-foot ranges. The local permits identify 286 wells in unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with additional wells in Laramie Fox Hills and Pierre Shale. In this Denver Basin sedimentary-bedrock setting, drilling conditions can change across short distances. Neighboring well logs are the best first check, but a driller still has to price for uncertainty, casing, grout, and the final completion depth.

sections.heading: What Rush wells produce
sections.html:
Among the 194 Rush-area wells that report a pump yield, the median is 10.2 gallons per minute. The middle half is 9.2 to 12.0 gallons per minute, and 79% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Another 14% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

No recorded wells in this set report less than 1 gallon per minute, while 7% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute. That is encouraging for household planning, but a pump test is still more useful than a countywide summary. Ask whether the reported figure is a short test or a sustained production rate, and confirm storage-tank sizing if the home, stock use, or irrigation demand will be significant.

sections.heading: Rush water levels and the recent measurement trend
sections.html:
The median static water level is 202 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half between 134 and 228 feet. That measurement is not the same as total well depth: a 280-foot well may have water substantially above its bottom, and pump placement must account for drawdown and recovery.

The decade medians show 165 feet below surface for measurements in the 2010s and 214 feet for measurements in the 2020s. That pattern suggests deeper measured water levels in the newer decade, but only 60 wells report static water levels, and the wells measured may not be the same wells or aquifers. Treat it as a reason to investigate, not proof of a uniform water-table decline across every Rush property.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Rush, and when
sections.html:
The permit history shows steady activity over many decades, with the newest permit year in 2025. The records contain 439 permitted wells, including 323 recorded as constructed. Permit counts rose from earlier decades, reached 84 in the 1990s, and include 60 permits in the 2020s.

Kunau Drilling LLC, associated in the records with Timothy R. Kunau, is the most frequent listed driller with 122 wells. Hamacher Well Works Inc., associated with Alan Ray Hamacher, appears on 100. Kunau Drilling & Excavation, associated with Harvey Kunau, appears on 28. These names show local permit history, not a recommendation. For a new project, confirm licensing, insurance, references, construction methods, and who will handle the permit and pump installation.

sections.heading: What a new Rush well may cost
sections.html:
For Rush ground identified as Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, the drilling rate model is $50 to $70 per foot. At the 280-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $14,000 to $19,600.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $20,000 to $31,600. That is a planning range, not a guaranteed bid. A deeper hole, difficult access, extra casing or grout, longer utility runs, a larger storage system, or unexpected formation conditions can move the final price. Ask each bidder to separate drilling, casing, grouting, pump equipment, electrical, trenching, testing, and permit-related work so proposals can be compared honestly.

sections.heading: Rush risks to check before building
sections.html:
Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles of Rush. That does not establish contamination at a particular well, but it is a reason to test existing water and review the location of any environmental site relative to the property. The records show no historic mine features and no EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within that mapped area.

Low-yield and dry-hole risk cannot be ruled out by a median. Confirm the well location, aquifer, construction report, pump test, and static water level before relying on a neighbor's result. Septic setbacks, driveway access, electrical routing, and building envelopes also need to be laid out together. Have the proposed septic system and well locations reviewed before excavation or a house plan is finalized.

sections.heading: A practical plan for buying land near Rush
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit records for the lot and nearby parcels, then compare total depth, aquifer name, static water level, yield, and use. The local use mix is heavily domestic or household, with stock use also common, so confirm that the existing permit supports the use you intend. Irrigation is uncommon in this record set.

For a vacant lot, get a driller's site review before closing if the well location is uncertain. Budget using the local depth and cost ranges, but keep room for a deeper completion and site work. Colorado permits control what an exempt household-use well can do, including the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit, and over-appropriated basins may require an augmentation plan. Verify current rules with DWR and your water attorney.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Rush, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Rush is 280 feet. The middle half runs from 175 to 360 feet, and the 90th percentile is 475 feet. Records range as deep as 600 feet. Most wells fall in the 100-to-300-foot or 300-to-600-foot groups, so nearby construction reports are important when estimating a new well.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Rush, Colorado?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $70 per foot. At the 280-foot median depth, drilling is estimated at $14,000 to $19,600. A finished well with a pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $20,000 to $31,600. Actual bids can change with access, casing, formation conditions, and final depth.

faq.q: How much water does a Rush well produce?
faq.a: Among 194 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 10.2 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 9.2 to 12.0 gallons per minute, and 79% report between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. No recorded wells report less than 1 gallon per minute, but a property-specific pump test remains essential.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Rush, Colorado?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish that every Rush well is safe to drink. Five PFAS sampling or contamination sites are mapped within about ten miles, so test a prospective home's water and review nearby environmental information. Also test for routine household concerns through a qualified laboratory rather than relying only on the well permit or a neighbor's result.

faq.q: Are Rush well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported static water levels were deeper below the surface in the 2020s than in the 2010s: the decade medians were 214 feet and 165 feet, respectively. Only 60 wells report static water levels, and the measured wells or aquifers may differ. The pattern warrants investigation, but it does not prove a uniform decline across every Rush property.
